Why American Military Doctrine Is Doomed For Failure

The TL;DR of this article essentially is that the US Navy is an obsolete sort of bluewater coast guard that can't actually do its job against any opponent that matches it in firepower.

The new generation of anti-ship missiles (DF-26, BrahMos II, Qader and P-900) offer a clear example of how Beijing and Moscow are reacting to the steady degradation of the frameworks for global peace. If the US Navy is denied a radius of several hundred kilometers, which is needed in order to control ships and aircraft carriers close to an enemy coast, this is a big problem for American military planners. The anti-ship missiles also offer an economic advantage: they cost little but can sink ships worth billions of dollars. They are thus ideal for challenging the US Navy, whose unparalleled power can be seen in its 10 aircraft carriers. Furthering this strategy, Russia and China are working on beyond-visual-range (BVR) missiles that, combined with stealth aircraft (J-20 and PAK FA), can deny the United States the essential ability to anticipate a lethal attack on its aircraft carriers that can be launched from a safe distance.

If you can't get an aircraft carrier safely close enough that its planes can reach their targets, that aircraft carrier -- and the entire flotilla of ships that must protect that carrier -- is useless. It assumes the same status as the battleship did by the second half of World War 2: a white elephant made obsolete by better airpower. This was precisely the lesson England learned when it decided to send the Sheffield and a bunch of other big floating targets to the Falklands and found out exactly how well Exocet missiles worked.

Smaller anti-ship missiles being cheaper also has another element to it, which is essentially the Zerg Rush: if a carrier group has capacity to destroy or fool X number of incoming missiles, all an opponent has to do to hit that carrier is send in X+1 missiles. This is another reason the US's enemies are so interested in mounting long-range missiles on piddling, tiny corvettes: you can deploy more missiles simultaneously. This is precisely the scenario that played out in Tom Clancy's Red Storm Rising, and one assumes he sort-of knew what he was talking about even back then. That's leaving aside the other weapon to which the US Navy carrier group has no answer and never did: a nuke detonated a couple of kilometres from a target.

Sure, the US Navy probably has a great record against countries like Afghanistan, which by definition doesn't have a navy. But using that as a justification to continue the silly big-boys-toys that carriers are is sort of like saying that because you have a cannon and can beat up the guy who only has a stick, the cannon is perforce adequate to beat every enemy you're going to face. As William Lind pointed out long ago -- the US Navy is basically organised to refight the Second World War. Its carriers are still patiently awaiting that last Japanese naval group sailing over the horizon.
